d6_arrive: Day six. Feel the guard. Yesterday you caught the tamperers, and inside each one you found a want — you saw that it was a want. Today you don't stop at seeing. You turn to the guard, and you feel its want as raw desire — the same quality you've been feeling all week. Safety, wanting. Reliability, wanting. Perfection, wanting. Not the note that a want is in there — the wanting itself, in the body. And one more thing you caught yesterday: a want and a fear arriving at the same instant, the fear closing the desire before it became anything at all. Today that instant is the practice. The sweep stays sparse — you opened only one instruction yesterday. The anchor is where the day lives. Timers start at zero. Begin when you're ready.
d6_soak1: First voice. Hudson, on the guard itself. There's nothing that you do that isn't based in a want. I'm sitting here having a conversation with you — there's a want to do that. And then he goes further: even if I was doing it out of obligation, then there is a want — for you not to abandon me.
d6_soak1_verify: So the obligation, the should, the guard — it isn't the absence of a want. It's a want wearing a rule. Under I have to is I want not to be abandoned. Yesterday you found the want inside the armor. Today you feel it.
d6_soak2: Second voice. Hudson again — the core instruction, the one he calls the most important of all of them. To feel wanting. To allow yourself to have the physical, emotional experience of wanting. To just sit in that — to bathe in it, to savor that feeling — and to do it without a subject at first. Just feel what it is to want.
d6_soak2_verify: Today the guard's want gets exactly this. Not named — bathed in. The safety, felt as wanting. The reliability, felt as wanting. The perfection, felt as wanting. The same raw quality you've found in the pelvis, the chest, the head — now in the guard. And your own catch, from yesterday: managing a want to make it reliable is a way to avoid feeling it. So feel the reliability itself, as a want — and it stops needing to manage.
d6_soak3: The last voice is yours, from yesterday. One useful way to describe them is competing wants. They just want something else — safety, reliability, perfection. And the strategy that seemed most helpful was to allow them to be fully felt as well. Viewing them as desire. — You viewed them as desire yesterday. Today you feel them as desire. Before the sit, one move: which guard do you already know? Name it now — the safety, the reliability, or the perfection you're most likely to reach for — so you'll recognize it when it moves.
d6_practice_intro: The sit. The sweep runs settle to whole body, then the anchor. Sparse still — the narration only names each station; you supply the instruction, from five days now. If one doesn't come, tap the instruction beside the dwell — it's counted, and that's fine. But keep it quick; today the anchor is the whole day. Set that one generously. The chime is permission, not a demand.
d6_prompt_sweep: The sweep, from recall. Anything to note before the anchor? Tap and speak — or continue.
d6_anchor: Many wants at once — and today, turning to the guard. This is the long one; this is the day. First, the ground. Let the wants of this actual day arise together — what you want from the rest of it, felt in the body, before any plan. All of them at once, moving freely, none suppressed. — Now the work. The guards will move; you know them now — a should, a not-now, a get-it-right-first. Yesterday you caught them and found the want each one guarded. Today you don't stop there. Turn toward the guard, and feel its want as raw desire — the same quality you've been feeling all week. The should is a want to be good. The not-enough-time is a want to be safe, to be enough. The get-it-right-first is a want for things to be reliable. Feel that wanting, in the body — bathe in it, no subject, the way you feel any want. Not the note that a want is in there. The wanting itself. — And the instant. Yesterday a want and a fear arrived together — the fear shutting the want down before it became anything. When that happens now, it's the practice, not the interruption. A want starts; something moves to close it — hold both. Don't let the guard finish its job. Feel the want that was beginning, and the guard's own wanting, side by side. Two wants — not a want and its executioner. — All of them on the same ground: the wants of the day, and the wanting inside every guard. One raw quality. Nothing to choose. Nothing to solve. Stay as long as you want.
d6_prompt_inventory: Name what you found. Which guard became a want — and what was the want inside it? Which one stayed armor, and wouldn't open? And did you catch the instant — a want and a fear at the same moment? Tap and speak.
d6_sayitback: Say it back. When you feel a guard's want as desire — instead of just noting it — what happens to the guard? In your own words. Tap and speak, when you're ready.
d6_sayitback_sources: The course's answer, to check against — not to grade. A guard is a want wearing a rule. Even obligation, Hudson says, is a want — a want for you not to abandon me. Noted, the guard stays a wall. Felt as desire — bathed in, no subject — the safety, or the reliability, or the goodness it was chasing turns out to be just more wanting, and it joins the others. The war doesn't end by defeating the guard. It ends by feeling what the guard wanted all along. And the instant: caught and held instead of obeyed, the want gets to become something before the guard can close it. Whatever you found is data for the build.
d6_close: That's the day. In the field, one situation to watch for: several things you want to do, and the thought arrives — there's not enough time. That verdict is a guard, and yesterday you watched it sour the wanting into dejection. When it comes, give it the ten seconds. Feel the not-enough as a want — to be enough, to do enough, to not fall short. Let it be wanting. Then see whether the dejection still comes. Export when you're ready. Day seven comes from what you found.
